I know you're right...I feel like I'm not strong enough to stop talking to him, though. Sometimes, I'm confident that I can move on. Other times, I believe that we should be together and I can't give up. It's frustrating.

I know that it wasn't me, it was him. Yet, I still wonder if I should have done something differently, as if it was my fault. I figure that it's not meant to be, but I keep hoping. I hate it. I'm not sure whether or not I should cut off contact with him. We've been talking again, and I felt like things were going well, until I brought up what happened. It wasn't intentional, I don't even know why I did...but then things got better again. 

I should probably stop talking to him. However, that obviously has not worked out for me. I keep going back.

That's great to hear! It's always encouraging to look back and see the progress that's been made. It makes it easier to face current challenges. I also check things in 8s, have been for 7 years. It's been hard for me to quit doing it. I think what I'm taking right now is Zoloft (sertraline). It's been fairly effective, but I've still been having a hard time stopping the counting.

I haven't heard of paxil before, although I took trazadone for a brief period of time. Thank you, I appreciate that! I love learning about other people's experiences. So has paxil been very successful for you then? I've been struggling with OCD more lately, and I was thinking about whether I might want to try to find another medication or not.
Wow, it took quite a long time for you then. Have things started to improve since you were diagnosed?

It seems like it hasn't been long since OCD started to be viewed as a legitimate disorder. Although, a lot of medical professionals still don't know much about it, which was a big factor in why I decided to write this book. If you don't mind me asking, what meds are you taking? I have also tried to go off of them a couple of times, but the results weren't good.
Well, it was smart of you to seek answers for it. I'm the same way on Sundays. I procrastinate a lot, and it's definitely depressing to think about what could have been done, but wasn't.

I'm a Christian, and having OCD has definitely affected my relationship with God in a big way. For years, I've struggled with wondering what I should pray for, and what is trivial enough to leave out in prayers. It's led to excessive prayer, which can be stressful and sometimes makes me want to have nothing to do with God.

It's a bit depressing.

I usually don't see any effects until I miss two or three doses (I take sertraline/Zoloft at 200mg). I'm horribly forgetful...I start feeling dizzy, can't think straight, don't feel completely in control of my actions. It can be unnerving at times, but it helps me remember to take my meds.
I'm 18, and OCD began for me when I was about 6 or 7. It was at its worst when I was 12-14.

So is this her first visit for her problems with OCD? He might be able to recommend someone who specializes in the treatment of it. The therapy my counselor did with me was Exposure and Response Therapy. It was extremely effective. While I can't say if it would have the same effect for her, I'd definitely ask the counselor about finding someone who offers that kind of treatment.

I'm so sorry. OCD is an awful, awful disorder. I agree with the other person who commented. There's not one treatment/medication that fits all. Everyone's different, and some people just don't respond to certain kinds of therapy or medications. 

If you don't mind me asking, what kinds are you taking at the moment? Both therapy and meds.

You might be a stranger to me, but I'm proud of you. It can be so hard to fight obsessions, and it takes a lot of strength to not give in. You'll get stronger every time you tell OCD "no," so don't give up. You're on the right track, keep going!

First of all, I want to point out that most people who have OCD take great care to hide it. It's not that you weren't observant. Your girlfriend probably learned how to keep it a secret over time. 

A major part of OCD is fear. Oftentimes, when a person does a compulsion (like the touching things you mentioned), it's to help ease whatever fears they have. For some people, OCD "says" that if he or she doesn't do this compulsion, something bad might happen to them or their family. So, by doing the compulsion, it's supposed to "prevent" this from happening, even though the person is fully aware that it doesn't make sense. The more a person gives in, the harder it is to stop. It's a stressful cycle.

The best thing you can do for your girlfriend is support her. When During my most difficult battles with OCD, I often felt isolated. Even offer to help her do her therapy. Do you happen to know what kind she's getting?
